passages.t: A very high mountain and a man with a measuring rod
passages.happening:
In the twenty-fifth year of the exile, the fourteenth year after Jerusalem fell, the hand of the LORD was on Ezekiel again. ‘In visions of God He took me to the land of Israel and set me on a very high mountain, on whose southern slope was a structure that resembled a city’ (verse 2). A man who looked like bronze stood in the gateway ‘with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand’ (verse 3). He told Ezekiel to look, listen and pay attention, and to report everything to the house of Israel (verse 4).

The man measured the wall around the temple area, then the east gate with its steps, its guardrooms and its porch, the outer court with its chambers, and the north and south gates, all with the same measurements (verses 5-27).
passages.hearers:
The date is about 573 BC. The beginning of the year and the tenth day may be the tenth of the first month, when Passover lambs were chosen, or the tenth of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement, depending on the calendar. Some scholars note that twenty-five years is half of the fifty-year cycle of the Jubilee, the year of release.

Ezekiel had known Solomon's temple, burned by the Babylonians. The gates he describes, with three chambers on each side of a long passage, closely resemble city gates of Israel's kings found by archaeologists at Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer. The measuring rod was six long cubits, a little over three meters. The plan is strikingly symmetrical, and the whole complex is a perfect square.
passages.later: Isaiah foresaw ‘the mountain of the house of the LORD’ raised above the hills (Isaiah 2:2). Zechariah saw ‘a man with a measuring line in his hand’ (Zechariah 2:1).
passages.hard:
Was this temple ever meant to be built, and how should the vision be read?

The temple of chapters 40 to 48 has never been built, and readers understand it in several ways; this site takes no side. Some take it as a real plan for the returning exiles that went unused, because the returned community lacked the means or did not meet the conditions of holiness the vision requires (43:10-11). Dispensational premillennial interpreters read it literally as a temple to be built in a future kingdom, with its sacrifices serving as memorials or for ceremonial purity rather than as atonement. Many other Christians, following a long tradition, read it as a symbol: the vision uses the familiar forms of temple and priesthood to picture God's perfect presence with a holy people, fulfilled in Christ, in the church, and in the new creation. Many scholars read it as an idealized vision, expressing in architecture what a holy, ordered community centered on God would be. Jewish tradition has generally expected a third temple in the age of the Messiah.

These readings differ on how the vision will be fulfilled, not on its center: the God who left a defiled temple will dwell again with his people in holiness. The vision makes no claim about any modern state, temple or border.
passages.asks: Ezekiel was told to look, listen and pay attention. Ask what it would mean to pay that kind of attention to God's presence. And ask what in your own life God might be measuring and claiming as his.

passages.t: The inner court, the altar and the porch
passages.happening: The man brought Ezekiel into the inner court by the south, east and north gates, each reached by eight steps and measured like the others (verses 28-37). There were rooms and tables for preparing the burnt offerings and the sin and guilt offerings (verses 38-43). Chambers were set apart for the singers and for the priests, one for those who keep charge of the temple and one for those who keep charge of the altar. ‘These are the sons of Zadok, the only Levites who may approach the LORD to minister before Him’ (verse 46). The inner court was a square, with the altar in front of the temple (verse 47). Ten steps led up to the porch of the temple, with pillars on each side (verses 48-49).
passages.hearers:
The tour moves inward and upward. Seven steps lead to the outer gates, eight to the inner gates, and ten to the temple porch. The prose is repetitive and technical on purpose; it slows the reader down. Measuring is itself a message: what God measures, he claims and protects.

Temples were often set on mountains, the meeting place of heaven and earth. The walls and gates separate zones of growing holiness, the outer court for the people, the inner court for the priests and the altar, and the sanctuary beyond. The sons of Zadok were the priestly family descended from Zadok, high priest under David and Solomon.
passages.later: Moses was told to make the tabernacle ‘according to the pattern I show you’ (Exodus 25:9). Solomon made Zadok priest in place of Abiathar (1 Kings 2:35).
passages.asks: Every step led higher and closer to the center. Ask what steps would bring you nearer to God this week. And ask what you need to leave behind at the gate.
